subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 18! This is a special project unit. Instead of only reading and answering questions, you are going to become a real probability investigator. You will ask a question about chance, make a careful guess about what will happen, run your own experiment, collect your own data, and then work out what your results tell you. By the end you will have carried out a whole investigation from the very first question to the final report, just like a true scientist.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 3 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Plan a simple probability investigation by choosing a clear question.
Make a sensible prediction (a hypothesis) before you begin.
Decide on your materials and how many trials to carry out.
Collect data neatly using tally charts and frequency tables.
Work out the experimental probability of an outcome (how often it happened out of all your trials).
Compare your results with the theoretical probability (what should happen in a fair test).
Draw a fair conclusion that answers your question using your data as evidence.
Present your findings clearly using tables, simple graphs and words.
Spot how probability is used in the real world all around you.

concepts.title: The Investigator's Cycle
concepts.explanation:
Every probability investigation, big or small, follows the same clear path. We call it the investigator's cycle because once you reach the end you can start again with a new question. Here are the six steps you will use again and again in this unit:

Predict what you think will happen, and why.

Experiment – plan it carefully and carry it out.

Record every result neatly as you go.

Analyse – count your results and work out the chances.

Conclude and present – answer your question and share it.

Think of it like preparing food for iftar during Ramadan. You decide what to cook (the question), you guess how long it will take (the prediction), you gather your ingredients and cook (the experiment), you taste and check as you go (recording), you judge whether it turned out well (analysing), and finally you serve it and tell the family how it went (presenting). A good investigator, like a good cook, never skips a step and never rushes.
concepts.example: Why follow the steps in order? Because each one rests on the one before. You cannot record results before you have run the experiment, and you cannot draw a fair conclusion before you have counted your data. Keeping to the order stops you from jumping to an answer too quickly – which is one of the most common mistakes in all of science. Let us now walk through each part of the cycle in more detail.

concepts.title: Asking a Good Question and Making a Prediction
concepts.explanation: Every investigation begins with a question. But not every question can be tested with an experiment. A good probability question is clear, is about chance, and can be tested by doing something many times. Compare these two questions: “Why is the sky blue?” cannot be tested by flipping or spinning, so it is not a probability question. But “When I roll a die, does each number come up about the same number of times?” is perfect – it is clear, it is about chance, and you can test it by rolling a die again and again. Once you have a good question, make a prediction – a sensible guess about what you think will happen, and why.
concepts.example: Is this coin fair? Does it land heads about as often as tails?

concepts.title: Planning a Fair Experiment
concepts.explanation:
Once you know your question and your prediction, you must plan the experiment. Good planning is what separates a trustworthy investigation from a messy one. Before you touch a coin or a die, decide these five things and write them in your journal:

What you will do – for example, flip a coin and look at which side lands up.

What counts as an outcome – here, heads or tails.

How you will record – usually a tally chart.

What materials you need – a coin, paper, and a pencil.

The most important planning decision is how many trials to do. A trial is one single try – one flip, one roll, one spin. If Farah flips a coin only four times and gets three heads, she cannot say the coin is unfair, because four trials is far too few. Chance needs room to settle down. The rule that investigators use is simple: the more trials you do, the more you can trust your results. For a coin or a die, at least 30 trials is a sensible minimum, and 50 or 100 is even better.

Why do more trials help? Imagine flipping a fair coin. In just a few flips you might, by luck, get mostly heads. But as you keep flipping, the good and bad luck start to balance out, and the number of heads creeps closer and closer to half. This is one of the most important ideas in all of probability: with only a few trials, luck rules; with many trials, the true chance shows itself. So an investigator who wants a reliable answer always plans plenty of trials.
concepts.example: You must also make your test fair. A fair test means nothing except chance decides the outcome. If Yusuf always drops the coin from the same low height and lets it spin, that is fair. But if he places the coin gently heads-up every time, he is not really testing chance at all. When drawing beads from a bag, a fair test means mixing the bag well and not peeking. When spinning a spinner, it means giving it a good, hard spin each time. Keeping the test fair is how you make sure your data is honest.

concepts.title: Collecting and Organising Your Data
concepts.explanation:
Now comes the exciting part – running the experiment and collecting data. Data is just a grown-up word for the results you gather. The secret to good data is to record it neatly and as you go, never from memory afterwards. The best tool for this is the tally chart.

A tally chart lets you count quickly without losing your place. Each time an outcome happens, you make one small vertical mark next to it. When you reach five, you draw the fifth mark across the other four, making a neat gate of five (IIII). Counting in fives like this is fast and hard to get wrong. Here is a tally chart Amina made while flipping a coin 20 times:

The last column shows the frequency of each outcome – that is, how many times it happened. Heads happened 11 times, tails happened 9 times, and 11 + 9 = 20, which matches the number of trials. Checking that your frequencies add up to your total trials is a smart habit; if they do not add up, you know a mark went missing somewhere.

When you have more than two outcomes, a frequency table keeps everything tidy. Here is one Hassan made while rolling a die 50 times. Each number from 1 to 6 has its own row, and the frequency column shows how many times it appeared:
concepts.example: Add the frequencies: 8 + 7 + 10 + 9 + 8 + 8 = 50. They add up to the total trials, so Hassan knows he recorded every roll. To organise data well, always group the same outcomes together, count the frequency of each, and check the total. A neat frequency table is the foundation of everything that comes next, because you cannot work out chances from messy, scattered marks.

concepts.title: Working Out Experimental Probability
concepts.explanation:
Once your data is collected and counted, you can work out the experimental probability of each outcome. This is the chance of an outcome based on what actually happened in your experiment. The rule is simple and you will use it many times:

Experimental probability = frequency ÷ total number of trials.

In words: take how many times an outcome happened, and divide it by how many trials you did altogether. Let us use Amina's coin data. She got 11 heads out of 20 flips, so the experimental probability of heads is 11 out of 20, which we can write as the fraction 11/20. Tails happened 9 times out of 20, so its experimental probability is 9/20. Notice that 11/20 and 9/20 add up to 20/20, which is one whole – because on every single flip, one of the two outcomes must happen.

Let us try Hassan's die. The number 3 came up 10 times out of 50 rolls, so its experimental probability is 10 out of 50. We can simplify 10/50 to 1/5. The number 2 came up 7 times, so its experimental probability is 7/50. Each outcome gets its own experimental probability, and all of them together add up to one whole, because every roll gives exactly one of the six numbers.
concepts.example: It helps to picture experimental probability as how big a share of the trials an outcome took. If green beads came out 14 times in 40 draws, green took a 14-out-of-40 share of the draws. You can even turn this into a comparison: 14 out of 40 is a bit more than a third, so green appeared a little more often than an equal share would give. Being able to say what your fractions mean in plain words is the mark of a real investigator.

concepts.title: Comparing With Theoretical Probability and Drawing Conclusions
concepts.explanation:
So far you have found the experimental probability – what actually happened. There is a second kind of chance called the theoretical probability – what should happen if everything is perfectly fair. For a fair coin, the theoretical probability of heads is exactly one half, because there are two equal sides. For a fair die, each number has a theoretical probability of one out of six, because there are six equal faces. For a fair four-colour spinner, each colour has a theoretical probability of one out of four.

The clever part of an investigation is comparing the two. If your experimental probability is close to the theoretical probability, your coin, die or spinner is probably fair. If it is far away, the object might be unfair – or you might simply need more trials. Let us look at a real example. A student spun a four-colour spinner 40 times and got these results:

Look carefully. Green came up more often than expected (0.35 against 0.25) and yellow came up less often (0.15 against 0.25). Does this prove the spinner is unfair? Not quite. With only 40 spins, some difference from the perfect quarter is completely normal – that is just luck at work. A wise investigator would say: “The results are a little uneven, but 40 spins may be too few to be sure. I would need many more spins before I could say the spinner is truly unfair.”
concepts.example: This is how you draw a conclusion. A conclusion answers your original question using your data as evidence. A good conclusion does five things: it answers the question directly, it uses the numbers as proof, it compares the result with the prediction, it admits any limitations (such as too few trials), and it may suggest a follow-up. Never say more than your data allows. Saying “the spinner is definitely broken” after only 40 spins is jumping too far; saying “green appeared a little more often, but I need more spins to be sure” is honest and scientific.

methods.title: How to run a probability investigation
methods.example: Idris says, “I wonder about my die.” Turn this into a clear, testable probability question.
steps: Ask a clear question about chance.
Make a prediction, with a reason.
Plan a fair experiment and choose plenty of trials.
Record every result with a tally chart.
Work out the experimental probability of each outcome.
Compare with the theoretical probability and draw a conclusion.
Present your findings with a table, a graph and clear words.

methods.title: How to make and read a tally chart
methods.example: Idris will roll his die 60 times. Write a prediction with a reason.
steps: Make one row for each possible outcome.
Add one mark each time an outcome happens.
Group the marks in fives (IIII) so they are easy to count.
Add up each row to find its frequency.
Check the frequencies add up to your total trials.

methods.title: How to draw a fair conclusion
methods.example: While flipping a coin, Farah records: Heads = IIII IIII IIII, Tails = IIII IIII. How many of each, and how many trials?
steps: Answer your question directly.
Use your numbers as evidence.
Compare the result with your prediction.
Admit any limitations, such as too few trials.
Suggest a follow-up investigation.

methods.title: Work out experimental probability
methods.example: Farah flipped a coin 30 times and got 18 heads. What is the experimental probability of heads?
steps: Use the rule: frequency ÷ total trials = 18 ÷ 30.
So the experimental probability of heads is 18/30, which simplifies to 3/5.
In plain words, heads came up on three out of every five flips.

methods.title: Compare with theoretical probability
methods.example: For Farah's coin above, the theoretical probability of heads is 1/2. Is her coin fair?
steps: Her experimental probability was 3/5, which is a little more than 1/2.
That is a small difference, and 30 trials is not very many, so we should say: “The coin looks roughly fair, but heads came up a bit more than expected.
I would flip it many more times to be sure.” We do not jump to calling it unfair.

methods.title: The most common total with two die
methods.example: Hassan rolls two dice and adds them. He wonders which total is most common. What should he expect, and why?
steps: The totals run from 2 to 12.
There are more ways to make 7 than any other total: 1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2 and 6+1 — six different ways.
No other total has six ways, so 7 should be the most common.
This is a prediction backed by a clear reason.

workedExamples.title: Turn an idea into a good question
workedExamples.prompt: Idris says, “I wonder about my die.” Turn this into a clear, testable probability question.
workedExamples.solution: A vague wonder must become a sharp question. A good version is: “Is my die fair — does each number from 1 to 6 come up about the same number of times?” This is clear, it is about chance, and Idris can test it by rolling the die many times and counting the results.

workedExamples.title: Make a prediction with a reason
workedExamples.prompt: Idris will roll his die 60 times. Write a prediction with a reason.
workedExamples.solution: “I predict each number will come up about 10 times, because 60 rolls shared fairly among 6 numbers gives 60 ÷ 6 = 10 each.” The reason (60 ÷ 6 = 10) turns the guess into real thinking. Notice the word “about” — a fair die will rarely give exactly 10 of each, but it should land close.

workedExamples.title: Read a tally chart
workedExamples.prompt: While flipping a coin, Farah records: Heads = IIII IIII IIII, Tails = IIII IIII. How many of each, and how many trials?
workedExamples.solution: Each gate of IIII is five. Heads has three gates: 5 + 5 + 5 = 15. Tails has two gates: 5 + 5 = 10. Total trials = 15 + 10 = 25. Always check the two frequencies add up to the number of trials.

workedExamples.title: Work out experimental probability
workedExamples.prompt: Farah flipped a coin 30 times and got 18 heads. What is the experimental probability of heads?
workedExamples.solution: Use the rule: frequency ÷ total trials = 18 ÷ 30. So the experimental probability of heads is 18/30, which simplifies to 3/5. In plain words, heads came up on three out of every five flips.

workedExamples.title: Compare with theoretical probability
workedExamples.prompt: For Farah's coin above, the theoretical probability of heads is 1/2. Is her coin fair?
workedExamples.solution: Her experimental probability was 3/5, which is a little more than 1/2. That is a small difference, and 30 trials is not very many, so we should say: “The coin looks roughly fair, but heads came up a bit more than expected. I would flip it many more times to be sure.” We do not jump to calling it unfair.

workedExamples.title: The most common total with two die
workedExamples.prompt: Hassan rolls two dice and adds them. He wonders which total is most common. What should he expect, and why?
workedExamples.solution: The totals run from 2 to 12. There are more ways to make 7 than any other total: 1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2 and 6+1 — six different ways. No other total has six ways, so 7 should be the most common. This is a prediction backed by a clear reason.

workedExamples.title: Draw a conclusion from a frequency table
workedExamples.prompt: A spinner with four equal colours is spun 40 times: Red 12, Blue 8, Green 14, Yellow 6. Write a fair conclusion.
workedExamples.solution: The theoretical probability of each colour is 1/4, so we would expect about 10 of each in 40 spins. Green (14) came up more and yellow (6) less. A fair conclusion is: “The spinner was a little uneven — green appeared most and yellow least — but with only 40 spins this may just be luck. More spins are needed before I could say it is truly unfair.”

workedExamples.title: Choose how many trials
workedExamples.prompt: Zahra wants reliable results when testing a coin. She asks whether 5 flips is enough. What should you tell her?
workedExamples.solution: Five flips is far too few — luck could easily give 4 heads and 1 tail by chance, which would fool her. Tell Zahra to do at least 30 flips, and 50 or 100 if she can, because the more trials she does, the closer her results will come to the true chance and the more she can trust them.

activities.title: The Great Coin Test
activities.materials: a coin (or a bottle cap), paper, a pencil.
steps: Write your question: ‘Is this coin fair?’ and your prediction with a reason.
Make a tally chart with two rows: Heads and Tails.
Flip the coin 50 times, making one tally mark each flip.
Count the frequency of each, then work out the experimental probability of heads (heads ÷ 50).
Compare with the theoretical probability of 1/2 and write a fair conclusion.

activities.title: Is My Die Fair? (Investigation)
steps: Write your prediction: about how many of each number in 60 rolls, and why.
Make a frequency table with a row for each number 1 to 6.
Roll the die 60 times, recording every roll with a tally mark.
Check your frequencies add up to 60, then work out each experimental probability.
Decide: does your die look fair, or do you need more rolls to be sure?

activities.title: The Mystery Bead Bag
activities.materials: a bag or cup, and beads, beans or stones in two or three colours.
steps: Put a secret mix of colours in the bag – have someone else choose the amounts.
Draw one out, record its colour with a tally, then put it back and mix well.
Repeat 40 times, keeping your tally neat.
Work out the experimental probability of each colour.
Guess how many of each colour are really in the bag, then look inside to check!

activities.title: Two-Dice Totals Race (Maths Game)
activities.materials: two dice, paper, a pencil, and a partner.
steps: Write the totals 2 to 12 across the top of your paper.
Predict which total will win by coming up most often, and say why.
Roll the two die, add them, and put a tally under that total.
Do 40 rolls, then see which total won the race.
Was your prediction right? Explain why 7 usually wins.

activities.title: Can You Beat Luck? (Family Task)
activities.materials: a coin, and several family members or friends.
steps: Ask each person to guess heads or tails before you flip.
Flip the coin and record whether their guess was correct or wrong.
Collect at least 50 guesses in a tally chart.
Work out the experimental probability of a correct guess.
Compare it with 1/2 (pure luck). Can people really beat chance, or not?

activities.title: Present Your Project
activities.materials: your results from any activity above, paper, and colours.
steps: Choose your favourite investigation from this unit.
Draw a bar graph with one bar for each outcome, coloured and labelled.
Write a short report: question, prediction, method, data, and conclusion.
Add one real-world link – who in real life uses chance like this?
Present it to your family or teacher and answer their questions.

rules.title: Experimental Probability Rule
rules.text: Experimental probability = frequency ÷ total number of trials. Example: 11 heads out of 20 flips = 11/20. All the experimental probabilities together add up to one whole.

rules.title: Theoretical Probability Rule
rules.text: Fair coin: 1/2 for heads, 1/2 for tails. Fair die: 1/6 for each of the six numbers. Fair four-colour spinner: 1/4 for each colour.

rules.title: More Trials Rule
rules.text: The more trials you do, the more you can trust your results. Do at least 30 trials; 50 or 100 is even better. A small difference from what you expect is usually just luck.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Working Out Experimental Probability.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Once your data is collected and counted, you can work out the experimental probability of each outcome. This is the chance of an outcome based on what actually happened in your experiment. The rule is simple and you will use it many times: Experimental probability = frequency ÷ total number of trials.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Comparing With Theoretical Probability and Drawing Conclusions.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
So far you have found the experimental probability – what actually happened. There is a second kind of chance called the theoretical probability – what should happen if everything is perfectly fair. For a fair coin, the theoretical probability of heads is exactly one half, because there are two equal sides. For a fair die, each number has a theoretical probability of one out of six, because there are six equal faces. For a fair four-colour spinner, each colour has a theoretical probability of one out of four.

The clever part of an investigation is comparing the two. If your experimental probability is close to the theoretical probability, your coin, die or spinner is probably fair. games.title: Spot the Error: Outcome
games.description: Practise outcome through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: What does “Probability” mean?
choices: How likely something is to happen
One single try of the experiment
A possible result of a trial
Marks that count / how many times it happened
rounds.answer: How likely something is to happen
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 18 Math Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: Probability means How likely something is to happen.

rounds.prompt: Which of these is a good, testable probability question?
choices: “Is this die fair?”
“Why is maths fun?”
“What is my favourite number?”
“Is the sky blue?”
rounds.answer: “Is this die fair?”
rounds.clue: Work it out yourself first, then look for your answer among the options.
rounds.explanation: A good probability question is clear, is about chance, and can be tested with an experiment.

rounds.prompt: A tally chart shows IIII IIII II for heads. How many heads is that?
rounds.clue: Rule out the options you know are wrong, then check the one that is left.
rounds.explanation: Each full gate of IIII is 5. Two gates (10) plus 2 more marks = 12.

rounds.prompt: A spinner is spun 40 times and lands on red 22 times out of 4 equal colours (expected about 10 each). What is a fair conclusion?
choices: Red came up more than expected, but more trials are needed before calling it unfair
Red is definitely unfair, no more testing is needed
The spinner cannot be tested
Red will always come up more than the other colours
rounds.answer: Red came up more than expected, but more trials are needed before calling it unfair
rounds.clue: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
rounds.explanation: A fair conclusion notes the difference from what was expected but does not jump to a firm decision without more trials.

games.title: Mastery Mix: Tally / Frequency
games.description: Practise tally / frequency through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: What does “Trial” mean?
choices: One single try of the experiment
A possible result of a trial
Marks that count / how many times it happened
Frequency ÷ total trials
rounds.answer: One single try of the experiment
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 18 Math Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: Trial means One single try of the experiment.

rounds.prompt: Idris will flip a coin 40 times. Which is the best prediction with a reason?
choices: “About 20 heads, because 40 shared fairly between 2 outcomes is 40 ÷ 2 = 20.”
“Exactly 20 heads, no more, no less.”
“I have no idea what will happen.”
“100 heads, because coins love heads.”
rounds.answer: “About 20 heads, because 40 shared fairly between 2 outcomes is 40 ÷ 2 = 20.”
rounds.clue: Work it out yourself first, then look for your answer among the options.
rounds.explanation: A good prediction gives a sensible number and explains the reasoning behind it.

rounds.prompt: A die is rolled 20 times and a 6 comes up 5 times. What is the experimental probability of rolling a 6?
rounds.clue: Rule out the options you know are wrong, then check the one that is left.
rounds.explanation: 5 out of 20 trials landed on 6, so the experimental probability is 5/20, which simplifies to 1/4.

rounds.prompt: Which is the best way to present the results of a chance experiment to others?
choices: A tally chart, a bar graph, and a short written conclusion
Just telling people the numbers from memory
Hiding the data so no one can check it
Only drawing a picture of the coin
rounds.answer: A tally chart, a bar graph, and a short written conclusion
rounds.clue: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
rounds.explanation: Presenting findings clearly means using tables, simple graphs and words together.

games.title: Unit Champion: Experimental probability
games.description: Practise experimental probability through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: What does “Outcome” mean?
choices: A possible result of a trial
Marks that count / how many times it happened
Frequency ÷ total trials
What should happen in a fair test
rounds.answer: A possible result of a trial
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 18 Math Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: Outcome means A possible result of a trial.

rounds.prompt: Before running an experiment, which of these should you decide?
choices: How many trials to do
What your favourite colour is
Who will win the football match
What the weather will be tomorrow
rounds.answer: How many trials to do
rounds.clue: Work it out yourself first, then look for your answer among the options.
rounds.explanation: Planning a fair experiment means deciding your materials and how many trials you will carry out.

rounds.prompt: A fair coin should land heads about half the time. In 50 flips, Farah gets 27 heads. Is this close to the theoretical probability?
choices: Yes, close to a half
No, nowhere close
It is exactly half
Cannot say without more information
rounds.answer: Yes, close to a half
rounds.clue: Rule out the options you know are wrong, then check the one that is left.
rounds.explanation: 27 out of 50 is close to 25 out of 50 (one half), so the result is close to the theoretical probability.

rounds.prompt: Which of these questions is NOT a good probability question?
choices: “Does this spinner land on each colour about equally?”
“What is my favourite colour?”
“Does this coin land heads about half the time?”
“Does this die land on 6 about one time in six?”
rounds.answer: “What is my favourite colour?”
rounds.clue: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
rounds.explanation: A favourite colour is a personal opinion, not something about chance that can be tested with trials.

selfAssessment: I can plan a simple probability investigation by choosing a clear question.
I can make a sensible prediction (a hypothesis) before you begin.
I can decide on your materials and how many trials to carry out.
I can collect data neatly using tally charts and frequency tables.
I can work out the experimental probability of an outcome (how often it happened out of all your trials).
I can compare your results with the theoretical probability (what should happen in a fair test).
I can draw a fair conclusion that answers your question using your data as evidence.
I can present your findings clearly using tables, simple graphs and words.
